title: Investor Sentiment
body:
**Investor sentiment** is the part of market behaviour coming from optimism, pessimism, fear,
excitement or social influence, with fundamentals accounting for the rest. The project's
research report uses the term for the component of a price that valuation cannot explain.

The central finding from the literature is that sentiment matters most where valuation is
hardest. Baker and Wurgler argue that sentiment has larger effects on securities that are
difficult to value and difficult to arbitrage, including young, small, unprofitable and
non-dividend-paying firms. A company with forty years of stable earnings has a defensible
price; a company with a story and no revenue has a price made of expectations.

That explains the pattern the case studies show, which is that the speculative corners of the
market are the emotional ones, and it makes sentiment a structural feature of the market.

Media tone is measurable evidence for it. Tetlock found that unusually pessimistic media tone
is followed by downward price pressure and then a rebound, which is the signature of sentiment
moving a price away from value and value pulling it back.

[[Herd Behavior]] and [[Narrative Contagion]] are the mechanisms that spread it, the
[[VIX]] is the market's own measure of expected fear, and [[Behavioral Finance]] is the
field studying it.
